analysis.one_liner: Closes offshore loopholes that let multinational corporations and wealthy individuals avoid U.S. taxes.
analysis.headline: Backed by 60 House Democrats, the bill never got a committee hearing or vote and died when the 115th Congress ended in January 2019.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it much harder for multinational corporations and wealthy individuals to hide income offshore. It expands reporting of foreign accounts, taxes income shifted to low-tax foreign affiliates, treats U.S.-managed foreign corporations as domestic, tightens rules on companies that invert (reincorporate abroad), and requires corporations to disclose their profits and taxes country by country. It also subjects investment advisers and company-formation agents to anti-money-laundering rules and lets Treasury restrict foreign banks that impede U.S. tax enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary U.S. taxpayers, who shoulder more of the tax burden when corporations and wealthy individuals shift profits and assets offshore; the IRS and Treasury, which gain enforcement tools like stronger John Doe summonses and presumptions against non-reporting foreign institutions; and investors and the public, who would see corporations' country-by-country profits and tax payments posted online.

how_it_helps.text: Expands reporting requirements for foreign investments and accounts and creates a rebuttable presumption that money moving through institutions that do not comply with FATCA reporting is taxable U.S. income, making hidden offshore accounts easier to catch.

Treats foreign corporations managed and controlled primarily in the United States as domestic for tax purposes, and tightens the rules on inverted corporations (companies that acquire foreign firms to reincorporate in low-tax countries), lowering the ownership threshold that triggers U.S. tax treatment to 80 percent.

Requires every SEC-registered corporation to file a public, online, country-by-country report of revenues, profits, income tax accrued and paid, employees, and assets, making profit-shifting to tax havens visible to the public.

Subjects investment advisers and people in the business of forming corporations and LLCs to anti-money-laundering obligations, and strengthens John Doe summons proceedings so the IRS can more easily obtain records of taxpayers using banks that refuse FATCA reporting.

Closes specific deduction and income-shifting channels, including taxing offshore swap payments as U.S.-source income, treating excess income from transfers of intangibles like patents to low-taxed affiliates as currently taxable, and limiting interest deductions of U.S. subsidiaries of foreign parent groups loaded with domestic debt.

analysis.who_pays: Multinational corporations that shift profits offshore, wealthy individuals using foreign accounts, offshore banks and financial institutions that decline to report to the IRS, investment advisers, and company-formation agents, who would face new taxes, reporting duties, and anti-money-laundering compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Multinationals, offshore banks, wealthy account holders

drawbacks.text: The bill layers substantial new compliance costs on multinational companies and financial institutions: country-by-country SEC reports, new IRS information returns, anti-money-laundering programs for advisers and formation agents, and complex new allocation rules for foreign deductions and taxes.

Its presumption provisions shift the burden of proof: money received from or transferred to an account at a non-reporting foreign institution is presumed taxable income, and the presumption can be rebutted only by clear and convincing evidence, which risks unfair treatment of account holders with legitimate transactions.

By unilaterally restricting foreign jurisdictions and institutions deemed to impede U.S. tax enforcement — including bans on correspondent accounts and card use in the U.S. — the bill could disrupt legitimate cross-border banking and business for customers who are not evading taxes.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core aim — making offshore profit-shifting and hidden accounts visible and taxable — would address a real revenue loss borne by ordinary taxpayers, and transparency measures like country-by-country reporting are low-cost relative to what they reveal. But the bill is blunt: its burden-shifting presumptions trade procedural fairness for enforcement power, and its web of new allocation, reporting, and anti-money-laundering rules would fall on companies and institutions of all kinds, with some costs likely passed to customers.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the House Ways and Means and Financial Services committees for the entire 115th Congress without a hearing, markup, or vote, and expired when the Congress ended in January 2019.

narrative.text: Rep. Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on April 5, 2017 with 57 original cosponsors, all Democrats, and 60 Democrats had signed on as cosponsors in total.
The House referred it to the Ways and Means Committee and, for relevant provisions, the Financial Services Committee; that referral on April 5, 2017 was the only action the bill ever received.
Neither committee ever held a markup or scheduled the bill, and it never reached the House floor before the 115th Congress ended on January 3, 2019.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Multinational corporations, offshore financial institutions, and holders of undeclared foreign accounts avoided the new taxes, reporting requirements, and enforcement tools; the Republican committee chairs were spared a vote on a measure their members did not support.

for.name: Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Stop Tax Haven Abuse Act and recruited the bill's cosponsors.

for.name: 60 of 194 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every recorded cosponsor was a Democrat and no Republican signed on.

against.name: Kevin Brady
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill after referral; the committee held no hearing or markup in the two years it had jurisdiction.

against.name: Jeb Hensarling
against.what_they_did: Took no action on the bill's securities, disclosure, and anti-money-laundering provisions after referral; no hearing or markup was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: All 60 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican cosponsor is recorded; with Republicans controlling both committees and the House agenda, the bill received no action after its April 2017 referral.

industries.note: The bill taxes income shifted to low-taxed foreign affiliates, limits interest deductions for debt-laden U.S. subsidiaries of foreign parents, and ends several deferral and check-the-box planning tools, directly reducing profits preserved through offshore structures. The revenue those structures shield is revenue ordinary taxpayers must otherwise make up.

industries.industry: Offshore banks and tax haven financial institutions
industries.note: Institutions that decline FATCA reporting face Treasury 'special measures' including bans on U.S. correspondent accounts and card transactions, and accounts held there trigger adverse tax presumptions for their U.S. customers. Their secrecy business depends on keeping enforcement at bay.

Advisers would have to run anti-money-laundering programs, file suspicious activity reports, and verify customers for the first time, with deadlines set in the bill. The burden is compliance-focused and applies to firms of all sizes.

Firms that form corporations, LLCs, and trusts would become subject to the Bank Secrecy Act, closing a channel long used to set up anonymous shell entities. Legitimate law firms using paid U.S. agents are excluded.

Every issuer would file a public country-by-country report of revenues, profits, and taxes paid, adding annual reporting work. Investors and the public gain visibility into where profits sit versus where taxes are paid.
